Communication design · Ghana & the United States

Johnson Kwame Wor

Design practice and teaching are the same job, done in two directions.

Two decades of design made for public space — billboards, packaging, campaign posters, book covers and identities produced in Ghana and the United States — and two decades teaching other people to make it.

I teach at Northern Illinois University, where I am Instructor of Record in Art and Design Education and finish my PhD in December 2026. My dissertation asks what happens when a design student's work is judged by cultural standards different from the ones that shaped it.

Before that, fourteen years in Ghanaian classrooms — Senior Lecturer at Takoradi Technical University, concurrently at the University of Education, Winneba — carrying most of the undergraduate communications design curriculum: foundations, visual design, illustration, photography, advertising and media planning.

Along the way I wrote and designed a graphic design textbook for Ghanaian colleges and universities, and was one of four people appointed to write Ghana's national graphic design and printing curriculum.

The practice came first. Creative Director at Cosmos Educational Press in Accra, then two years running a university printing press — which is where I learned what a file does after it leaves the designer's hands. I trained at KNUST in Kumasi: BFA in Graphic Design, MA in Publishing Studies.

The through-line has not changed: design that has to work in public, for people who did not commission it and will not read a caption.

Selected work

Eleven projects
2004 – 2025

Outdoor & campaign

One identity, three formats — and three different jobs to do.

The can

The constant. Condensation, a hand-drawn wordmark and a two-tone split that survives being shrunk to a shelf facing or blown up to two metres.

The poster

Gives the can a stage. The chequered plane, suspended fruit and running figure argue the health claim rather than the stimulant one — a category convention turned to a different end.

The banner

Drops the argument entirely. At ten metres a shopper wants the flavour range and a number to call, so the narrative gives way to an inventory.

Teaching

Ghana & the U.S.
2007 – present

I teach graphic design as a way of thinking, not a set of skills to acquire.

Tools change and platforms come and go; the software a student masters in their sophomore year may be obsolete by graduation. What lasts is the ability to see a problem clearly, make deliberate visual decisions, defend them, and adapt when the situation shifts.

The studio is a working community, not a room where I lecture and students execute. Critique sits at the centre of everything I do, and I treat it as a skill students learn rather than a verdict they receive. Early in a course I model how to look at work and name what is happening in it. By the end I want students running their own critiques, articulating their choices, and unafraid to question mine.

I have taught this way for close to two decades — to fourth-graders learning to see line and shape, to undergraduates in Ghanaian design studios, and to graduate students in the United States unpacking the philosophy behind assessment.

Research

Assessment · Critique
Cross-cultural pedagogy

When a design is judged, whose standards are doing the judging?

My research grew out of my own working life. Having taught design for close to two decades in Ghana and now in the United States, I have watched the same layout, the same drawing, the same critique land completely differently depending on where the student and the instructor came from.

That gap is the centre of my scholarship, and it matters for anyone who teaches, assesses and mentors art and design students.

The dissertation. A cross-cultural qualitative study of how cultural difference shapes assessment and critique in undergraduate graphic design classrooms in Ghana and the United States, and how those practices can become more culturally responsive.

Framework. Gloria Ladson-Billings' culturally responsive pedagogy, supported by Hofstede's cultural dimensions, Hall's work on high- and low-context communication, and postcolonial theory.

Method. Reflexive thematic analysis across interviews, focus groups, classroom observations, syllabi and rubrics, and students' design work.

One thread I find especially generative: minimalist Western design tends to read as neutral, while non-Western design gets labelled as cultural — a framing that quietly shapes what counts as good work.
